name: SecureDrop
purpose: Whistleblower submission system where sources upload documents and messages over a Tor onion service to hardware controlled by the news organisation, with per-source codenames, no accounts and an air-gapped decryption model.
journalism_use_case: The reference system for receiving documents from a source who must not be identifiable, including by the news organisation itself: the source connects over Tor, receives a codename rather than an account, and submissions are decrypted on an air-gapped machine so a server compromise does not expose plaintext.
pros: Threat model is explicit and unusually honest: it is designed on the assumption that the server will be seized or compromised, which is why decryption is air-gapped rather than server-side
Tor onion service means no IP address is exposed to the newsroom or its hosting provider, so the organisation cannot be compelled to produce what it never had
Maintained by an organisation whose sole purpose is press freedom, with regular releases (2.16.2, 2026-10-29), published security audits and a documented support process
Codename-based pseudonymity avoids collecting any source identifier at all — the strongest available posture against legal compulsion
cons: Heavy operational requirement: dedicated hardware (application server, monitor server, air-gapped Secure Viewing Station), physical security, and a maintenance routine — this is an institutional commitment, not a deployment
Journalists must actually use the workstation discipline, and the system's security collapses if submissions are copied onto an ordinary laptop — the human failure mode dominates the technical one
GitHub reports SPDX NOASSERTION (the project is AGPL-3.0 per its own licensing) and carries 479 open issues, reflecting a large, complex system
Sources must find and trust the onion address, so publicising it safely is part of the work, and a source using Tor in a hostile country may itself attract attention
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 3,896 stars with 479 open issues, release 2.16.2 (2026-10-29), pushed 2026-11-14; session 1's ground_truth.tsv independently recorded AGPL-3.0 and the same release line. SecureDrop's deployment by major news organisations is publicly documented by FPF, and the project publishes independent security audits — the strongest assurance evidence in this catalogue.
assessment: If your organisation intends to solicit documents from sources at real risk, this is the standard and I would adopt it — but only with the institutional commitment it requires, because a half-maintained SecureDrop is worse than none (it implies a protection it does not deliver). For an exile outlet the specific advantage is that it minimises what you hold: you cannot be compelled to produce source identities you never collected. If you cannot meet the operational bar, Hush Line or an OnionShare-based workflow is the honest fallback, and you should say publicly what protection you do and do not offer.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-14, latest release 2.16.2 (2026-10-29), 3,896 stars, 479 open issues. Regular versioned releases, a dedicated institutional maintainer (FPF), published security audits and a documented vulnerability-disclosure process — maintenance assessed on security process, not commit count.
licence: AGPL-3.0 (project's own licensing; GitHub API reports NOASSERTION)
licence_restrictions: AGPL-3.0: a modified instance offered over a network obliges source publication. Running the released version for your own newsroom carries no obligation. Do not fork quietly — security-critical modifications should go upstream.
costs: No software fee. Real costs are hardware and staff: two servers plus an air-gapped Secure Viewing Station and a dedicated USB workflow (low four figures in hardware, estimate), a Tor-reachable hosting arrangement, and — dominantly — ongoing administrator time for updates and a journalist-training routine. Budget this as a permanent staffed service rather than a project.
privacy: The strongest privacy design in this catalogue: Tor onion service (no source IP), no accounts (no identifiers), air-gapped decryption (no plaintext on a networked machine). Residual risks are real and must be managed: source-side risk from using Tor in a hostile network, metadata inside submitted documents (run Dangerzone and mat2), and the organisational discipline of never moving submissions onto ordinary devices.
alternatives: Hush Line for a far lighter encrypted tip line where SecureDrop's operational bar cannot be met
GlobaLeaks for a more configurable whistleblowing platform used widely by NGOs and public bodies
OnionShare for one-off direct transfers between two people who are already in contact
blockers: Requires dedicated hardware, an air-gapped workstation and permanent administrator capacity — a partial deployment is actively misleading to sources
summary: Whistleblower submission system where sources upload documents and messages over a Tor onion service to hardware controlled by…
additional_costs_note: dedicated hardware; self-hosted infrastructure; staff effort

name: SecureDrop Workstation
purpose: Qubes OS-based journalist workstation for handling SecureDrop submissions, isolating networking, decryption, document viewing and export into separate virtual machines.
journalism_use_case: Replaces the air-gapped Secure Viewing Station with a single Qubes laptop where submissions are decrypted in one compartment, converted in another and read in a third — making the secure workflow something a journalist can plausibly follow daily rather than a procedure they avoid.
pros: Addresses the real failure mode of classic SecureDrop: the air-gapped workflow is onerous enough that journalists route around it, and compartmentalised-on-one-laptop is far more likely to be used as designed
Qubes compartmentalisation means a malicious document that executes affects a disposable VM, not the journalist's machine — the same protection Dangerzone gives, applied structurally
AGPL-3.0 and actively maintained (1.9.0, 2026-09-02; pushed 2026-11-16) by the same organisation as SecureDrop, so the pieces are designed together
Documented, opinionated configuration reduces the chance of a newsroom improvising an insecure setup
cons: Requires Qubes OS on certified hardware, which is a narrow hardware compatibility list and a significant procurement constraint
268 open issues against only 189 stars — a high ratio indicating a complex system with a small user base, so you will encounter unresolved problems
Qubes itself has a real learning curve; a journalist needs training and ongoing support, and the project does not remove that
Still bound to a SecureDrop deployment, so it adds to rather than replaces the institutional commitment
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 189 stars with 268 open issues, release 1.9.0 (2026-09-02), pushed 2026-11-16, AGPL-3.0. FPF documents it as the recommended journalist-side workflow for SecureDrop, which is the relevant institutional signal.
assessment: Adopt it alongside SecureDrop rather than as an alternative — the usability gain over the air-gapped SVS is the difference between a protocol that is followed and one that is nominally in place. For your profile the gating factor is hardware: confirm certified Qubes machines are procurable where you operate before committing, because in some exile contexts importing specific laptop models is itself difficult. Budget training time; Qubes is not intuitive.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release 1.9.0 (2026-09-02), 189 stars, 268 open issues. Current commits and versioned releases under institutional maintenance; the backlog reflects system complexity and a small contributor pool.
costs: No software fee. Qubes-certified laptop per journalist handling submissions (estimate: upper four figures for a small team), plus training and support time. Replaces the SVS hardware cost rather than adding to it.
privacy: Compartmentalised handling keeps decryption, viewing and export isolated, so a malicious submission cannot reach the journalist's general environment. Residual risk is the journalist's own operational discipline and the physical security of the laptop.
alternatives: Classic air-gapped Secure Viewing Station if Qubes hardware is unobtainable
Dangerzone on an ordinary machine as a much weaker but far more available mitigation
Tails on a USB stick for ad-hoc isolated document handling
blockers: Requires Qubes-certified hardware; narrow compatibility list
summary: Qubes OS-based journalist workstation for handling SecureDrop submissions, isolating networking, decryption…
additional_costs_note: dedicated hardware; self-hosted infrastructure; staff effort

name: Dangerzone
purpose: Desktop application that converts potentially malicious PDFs, Office documents and images into safe PDFs by rendering them to pixels inside an isolated container and rebuilding a clean file, with optional OCR to restore a text layer.
journalism_use_case: The step before any other tool in this catalogue touches a document from an unknown source: a file is sanitised so opening it cannot execute an exploit or beacon out to the sender. That protects the reporter's machine and, just as importantly, prevents a document from signalling to its originator that it has been opened — which can expose that a leak is being investigated.
pros: Addresses a threat that is real and routinely ignored: weaponised documents sent to journalists are a documented attack vector, and ordinary antivirus does not reliably stop a targeted exploit
The pixel round-trip is a structural rather than detection-based defence — it does not need to recognise the exploit to neutralise it, which is why it works against unknown attacks
Fully local by design: the whole premise is that nothing is uploaded and the conversion is isolated from the host, which distinguishes it from cloud sanitisation services
Actively maintained (v0.11.1, 2026-10-22; pushed 2026-11-09) by FPF with a journalism-specific threat model and installable builds for all desktop platforms
cons: The pixel round-trip destroys the text layer unless OCR is enabled, and the OCR'd text is then only as accurate as Tesseract — so sanitised documents are worse for search and quotation than originals, and teams are tempted to skip it
Conversion is slow on large documents, which again creates pressure to bypass it on exactly the big leaked set where it matters most
Container runtime dependency (Docker or Podman) complicates installation on managed or locked-down machines
AGPL-3.0 affects redistribution of a modified version; 193 open issues reflect the breadth of document formats in the wild
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 5,850 stars with 193 open issues, release v0.11.1 (2026-10-22), pushed 2026-11-09, AGPL-3.0 (independently recorded in session 1's ground_truth.tsv). FPF builds it specifically for journalists, and the threat it addresses — malicious documents targeting newsrooms — is documented in published threat reporting.
assessment: Adopt it as a mandatory first step and automate it so the choice is not left to a tired reporter at midnight: ingest pipelines should sanitise on arrival, keeping the original in a quarantined store for later forensic examination. For your profile the detail that matters most is preserving both artefacts — the sanitised copy for reading and the untouched original for analysis — because the original is evidence about the sender and discarding it loses that. Enable OCR, and accept the accuracy cost rather than skipping sanitisation.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-09, latest release v0.11.1 (2026-10-22), 5,850 stars, 193 open issues. Regular releases from an institutional maintainer with a security-focused mission; session 1 independently verified the same licence and release line.
licence_restrictions: AGPL-3.0: distributing a modified version or offering it as a service obliges source publication. Desktop use is unaffected.
costs: No fee. A container runtime and CPU time — conversion is the cost, measured in minutes per large document. No paid dependencies. For a large leak, budget compute time in the ingest plan.
privacy: Fully local — nothing is uploaded and the conversion is isolated from the host. This is the correct architecture and the direct contrast with commercial document-sanitisation services, which would receive your source documents.
alternatives: Opening documents inside a disposable Qubes VM or a Tails session for equivalent isolation without the text-layer loss
A dedicated offline examination machine, which is slower but preserves fidelity
Commercial sanitisation services — avoid, since they require uploading source documents
summary: Desktop application that converts potentially malicious PDFs, Office documents and images into safe PDFs by rendering them to…

name: OnionShare
purpose: Desktop and CLI tool that uses Tor onion services to share files, receive files, host a static website or run an ephemeral chat room directly between participants, with no intermediary server.
journalism_use_case: Direct, serverless transfer between a reporter and a source who are already in contact: the source runs OnionShare and sends a one-time onion address, the reporter downloads, and no third-party service ever holds the file or the metadata. The receive mode also gives a lightweight drop box without SecureDrop's infrastructure.
pros: No intermediary at all — the file goes device to device over Tor, so there is no provider to subpoena, no account, and no retained copy
Receive mode provides a usable drop box in minutes, which is the right tool when a source materialises and you have no SecureDrop

Licence corrected in this survey: the project's own LICENSE.txt is GPL-3.0 (GitHub's NOASSERTION is caused by a prepended note pointing to bundled third-party licences, which is what produced session 1's incorrect reading)
Very actively maintained (v2.7.2, 2026-11-07; pushed 2026-11-16) with 7,238 stars and a small backlog (63 open issues)
cons: Both parties must be online simultaneously for a transfer, which is a real coordination problem across time zones and for sources with intermittent connectivity
Requires the source to install and run software and to understand onion addresses — a meaningful barrier for a non-technical source under stress
Using Tor may itself be conspicuous on a monitored network, so in some countries the act of running OnionShare carries risk even though the transfer is protected
Nothing protects against metadata inside the transferred documents, so mat2 and Dangerzone remain necessary afterwards
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 7,238 stars with 63 open issues, release v2.7.2 (2026-11-07), pushed 2026-11-16. The licence question is resolved with primary evidence: LICENSE.txt opens with '(Note: Third-party licenses can be found under licenses/.)' followed by the OnionShare copyright and the full GPL-3.0 text — recorded in sources/evidence/leads.md as lead L8.
assessment: Adopt as the standard answer for ad-hoc secure transfer, and specifically teach reporters the receive mode — it is the fastest route from 'a source has documents' to 'we have them, with no intermediary'. For your profile the operational caveats to brief are the simultaneity requirement and the conspicuousness of Tor in some networks; where the latter matters, a bridge or a pre-arranged time window helps. Always follow a transfer with Dangerzone and mat2 before the documents touch anything else.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-16, latest release v2.7.2 (2026-11-07), 7,238 stars, 63 open issues. Frequent releases with a clean tracker; long-standing project with a security-literate maintainer base.
licence: GPL-3.0 (project's own LICENSE.txt read directly 2026-11-17; GitHub reports NOASSERTION because a note about bundled third-party licences is prepended to the GPL text)
model_or_data_licence: n/a. Third-party components under licenses/ have their own terms and must not be read as the project licence — this was the cause of session 1's misidentification.
licence_restrictions: GPL-3.0 on the project's own code; immaterial for ordinary use.
costs: Free. No infrastructure — the point is that there is no server. Bandwidth only.
privacy: Among the strongest in the catalogue: no intermediary, no account, ephemeral onion address, nothing retained after the transfer. Residual risks are the conspicuousness of Tor on a monitored network and document metadata, neither of which OnionShare addresses.
alternatives: SecureDrop where sources must be protected from the newsroom itself and cannot coordinate live
Hush Line for asynchronous encrypted tips
Signal for messages and small files between parties who can both install it
summary: Desktop and CLI tool that uses Tor onion services to share files, receive files…

name: GlobaLeaks
maintainer: Hermes Center for Transparency and Digital Human Rights
purpose: Configurable whistleblowing platform supporting anonymous submissions over Tor or HTTPS, multi-tenant deployments, customisable questionnaires, case management and multilingual interfaces.
journalism_use_case: A whistleblowing channel you can shape to the reporting context: unlike SecureDrop's deliberately minimal model, GlobaLeaks lets you build structured intake (questionnaires, categories, recipient routing), which suits a newsroom running several tip lines or a consortium where submissions must route to different partners.
pros: Configurability and multi-tenancy are the distinguishing features: one deployment can serve multiple outlets or desks with separate recipients, which matters for consortium investigations
Supports both Tor and HTTPS access, so a source who cannot use Tor still has a protected channel — broader reach than Tor-only systems, at a stated cost in anonymity
AGPL-3.0, very actively maintained (v5.0.101, 2026-10-28; pushed 2026-11-17), with a long deployment history across NGOs, anti-corruption bodies and public institutions
Repository renamed (globaleaks/globaleaks → globaleaks/globaleaks-whistleblowing-software, transfer verified by redirect), so the canonical path is current
cons: The HTTPS option is a genuine trade-off, not just convenience: a submission over HTTPS exposes the source's IP to the hosting path, so the default must be understood and the choice explained to sources
620 open issues — the largest backlog in this subcategory — reflecting a broad feature surface and configurability that can be misconfigured
Decryption happens on the platform rather than on an air-gapped station, so a compromised server is a more consequential event than with SecureDrop's model
Configuration flexibility means security depends on your choices; a badly configured GlobaLeaks can retain far more than it should
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 1,529 stars with 620 open issues, release v5.0.101 (2026-10-28), pushed 2026-11-17, AGPL-3.0; repository transfer confirmed by API redirect on 2026-11-17. GlobaLeaks' use by anti-corruption authorities and NGOs is documented by the project, which is relevant institutional adoption evidence.
assessment: The right choice when you need structured intake or multi-recipient routing and can accept a weaker threat model than SecureDrop's; the wrong choice if your sources face state-level adversaries and you want minimal retained data. For your profile the decisive question is who you are protecting sources from: GlobaLeaks protects against opportunistic exposure and gives you workflow, while SecureDrop is built for the case where the newsroom itself may be compelled. Document which model you are offering, publicly and accurately.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v5.0.101 (2026-10-28), 1,529 stars, 620 open issues. Same-day commits and a very frequent release cadence under an established non-profit maintainer.
licence_restrictions: AGPL-3.0: a modified instance offered over a network obliges source publication. Relevant if you customise the platform for partners, which is a common GlobaLeaks use.
costs: No software fee. Infrastructure estimate: a hardened VM or dedicated server with Tor and HTTPS endpoints, plus encrypted storage — modest hardware, but security-critical hosting and permanent administrator attention. Assumptions: single-tenant newsroom deployment.
privacy: Tor submissions give no IP to the newsroom; HTTPS submissions do expose source IPs to the network path, which must be communicated to sources rather than left implicit. Server-side decryption means a seized or compromised server is a serious event — plan key handling and retention accordingly.
alternatives: SecureDrop where the threat model requires air-gapped decryption and minimal retained data
Hush Line for a lightweight encrypted tip line
OnionShare receive mode for ad-hoc intake with no platform at all
blockers: HTTPS submission path exposes source IPs; server-side decryption weakens the seizure threat model relative to SecureDrop
summary: Configurable whistleblowing platform supporting anonymous submissions over Tor or HTTPS, multi-tenant deployments…

name: Hush Line
purpose: Lightweight anonymous tip-line service with end-to-end encryption to the recipient's PGP key, usable as a hosted service or self-hosted, with optional Tor onion access.
journalism_use_case: The realistic middle option between an email address and SecureDrop: a reporter publishes a Hush Line address, tips arrive encrypted to their key, and no infrastructure project is required. For a small outlet or an individual journalist, this is the difference between having a protected channel and having none.
pros: Fills the gap that matters most in practice — most journalists have no protected tip channel at all because SecureDrop is too heavy, and this is deployable by one person
End-to-end encryption to the recipient's PGP key means the service operator cannot read tips, which is the key property for a hosted option
AGPL-3.0, actively released (v0.7.36, 2026-11-05) with a small clean backlog (13 open issues), self-hostable if you prefer not to rely on the hosted service
Tor onion access available, so a source with a serious threat model gets network-level protection too
cons: Smaller and younger than the alternatives (136 stars), so it has far less independent security scrutiny than SecureDrop — which matters for software in a source-protection path
Hosted mode means the operator sees metadata (when tips arrive, to whom) even though content is encrypted, and that metadata can be revealing
Depends on the journalist managing a PGP key correctly, which is historically where encrypted-tip workflows fail
Session 1's candidate path (freedomofpress/hushline) is a 404 — the project is at scidsg/hushline, which is worth noting since the wrong path appears in older notes
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 136 stars with 13 open issues, release v0.7.36 (2026-11-05), pushed 2026-11-14, AGPL-3.0. The corrected repository path (scidsg/hushline, not freedomofpress/hushline) was established in this session's 404 sweep and is recorded in leads.md.
assessment: Adopt it for individual reporters and small desks that will not run SecureDrop — a protected channel that exists beats a perfect one that does not. For your profile I would self-host rather than use the hosted service so the arrival metadata stays with you, and I would pair deployment with actual PGP key management support for the journalists involved, because that is the step that silently fails. Be honest in public about the protection level: it is not SecureDrop, and sources at state-level risk should be directed accordingly.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-14, latest release v0.7.36 (2026-11-05), 136 stars, 13 open issues. Frequent releases and a clean tracker from a small organisation; young project, so maintenance is assessed on cadence rather than track record.
licence_restrictions: AGPL-3.0: a modified hosted instance obliges source publication.
costs: Self-hosting: a small VM plus a Tor onion service — low. The hosted service has free and paid tiers whose current prices were NOT verified in this survey. Staff cost is PGP key management and monitoring the channel.
privacy: Content is end-to-end encrypted to the recipient's key, so even a hosted operator cannot read tips. Hosted mode still exposes arrival metadata to the operator; self-hosting removes that. Tor access protects source network identity where available.
alternatives: SecureDrop where the threat model justifies the operational commitment
OnionShare receive mode for a zero-infrastructure drop box
A published Signal number, which is simpler but requires the source to reveal a phone number
summary: Lightweight anonymous tip-line service with end-to-end encryption to the recipient's PGP key…
additional_costs_note: optional paid hosting / commercial licence; self-hosted infrastructure; staff effort

name: mat2
purpose: Metadata removal tool supporting a wide range of file formats — images, documents, audio, video, archives — that strips identifying metadata and can report which formats are supported on the current system.
journalism_use_case: The counterpart to verification: strip identifying metadata from images and documents before publishing or sharing them, so a published photo does not burn the source's device, location or filesystem trail. This is the step that has repeatedly failed in real cases where published files carried GPS coordinates or author names.
pros: Breadth of format support means one tool covers the realistic range of files a newsroom publishes, rather than needing per-format handling
Addresses a documented and recurring failure mode — published files leaking source-identifying metadata — with a simple, auditable intervention
LGPL-3.0-or-later with exemplary maintenance: release 0.15.0 (2026-08-04), pushed 2026-11-15, and only 2 open issues against 394 stars
Fully local processing, and `--check-dependencies` tells you honestly which formats your installation can actually clean
cons: Cleaning is best-effort and format-specific: unsupported formats may be refused or incompletely cleaned, so a silent partial clean is possible and you must check the tool's own report rather than assume success
It cannot remove information in visible pixels — reflections, screen contents, identifiable surroundings, visible badges — which is a frequent and more serious disclosure route than metadata
Per-format system library dependencies mean capability varies by installation, so a clean on one machine is not evidence of a clean on another
CLI-oriented; a reporter needs either training or a wrapper, and the ones who most need it are least likely to use a terminal
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 394 stars with 2 open issues, release 0.15.0 (2026-08-04), pushed 2026-11-15, LGPL-3.0 (independently recorded in session 1's ground_truth.tsv). The canonical home is 0xacab.org (GitLab) with the GitHub repository as the primary mirror; session 1's candidate paths 0xacab/mat2 and rhaberkorn/mat2 are both 404s, verified in this session.
assessment: Adopt and automate it into the publication path rather than relying on anyone to remember — metadata stripping is a checklist item that fails exactly when people are rushing to publish. For your profile the essential complement is a visual review step: mat2 handles the metadata, a human must handle what is visible in the frame, and in source-protection terms the pixels are usually the bigger risk. Record which formats your installation supports so you know what is actually being cleaned.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-15, latest release 0.15.0 (2026-08-04), 394 stars, 2 open issues. Near-zero backlog with current commits — excellent single-maintainer discipline over many years.
licence_restrictions: LGPL-3.0-or-later: linking from a proprietary tool is permitted provided the library remains replaceable; modifications to mat2 itself must be shared. Suitable for building a newsroom wrapper around.
costs: No fee. Per-format system libraries; negligible compute. No paid dependencies.
privacy: Fully local processing — nothing uploaded, which is the point for source-protection work. The limitation to state plainly to colleagues: it cleans metadata, not content.
alternatives: ExifTool for inspecting what metadata exists before and after cleaning
Dangerzone, whose pixel round-trip incidentally removes most metadata along with active content
PyMuPDF for true redaction of visible content in PDFs
summary: Metadata removal tool supporting a wide range of file formats — images, documents, audio, video, archives…

name: MVT (Mobile Verification Toolkit)
maintainer: MVT Project (Amnesty International Security Lab lineage)
purpose: Forensic toolkit that acquires and analyses iOS backups and filesystem dumps and Android device data, checking them against indicators of compromise for mercenary spyware such as Pegasus and Predator.
journalism_use_case: The standard tool for answering 'has this journalist's phone been targeted?' — running a consensual check on a reporter's or source's device against published spyware indicators, which is how most publicly confirmed Pegasus infections of journalists have been established.
pros: The reference implementation in this field, with direct lineage to the Amnesty Security Lab work that exposed Pegasus targeting of journalists — provenance no alternative matches
Works against standard iOS backups, so a check can be run without jailbreaking or specialist hardware, which makes consensual checks practical in the field
Very actively maintained (v2026.11.2, 2026-11-02; pushed 2026-11-17) with 16,096 stars and a modest backlog (66 open issues)
Indicator-driven: pair it with Amnesty's published IOCs and stalkerware-indicators to extend coverage beyond mercenary spyware
cons: LICENCE BLOCKER, verified with primary evidence: MVT License 1.1 §3.0 imposes a Consensual Use Restriction requiring the Data Owner's explicit, uncoerced and fully informed consent, including disclosure of privacy implications and the data-retention policy. This is a contractual obligation, not merely ethics, and it is not an OSI licence
A clean result is not evidence of safety: MVT finds known indicators, so a novel or well-cleaned implant is invisible, and reporting 'no infection found' as 'not targeted' would be wrong
iOS coverage is substantially better than Android, where acquisition is harder and artefacts are fewer — so Android results are weaker and need androidqf plus more care
Interpreting output requires forensic literacy; a false positive communicated badly to a journalist causes real distress, and a missed detection creates false confidence
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. The decisive documented fact is the licence, read in full from the repository: MVT License 1.1 §3.0 quoted verbatim in sources/evidence/leads.md with the full text saved at sources/recovered/cat/mvt.txt. 16,096 stars with 66 open issues; release v2026.11.2 (2026-11-02). MVT's role in confirmed Pegasus cases is publicly documented by Amnesty International.
assessment: Adopt it, and build the licence obligation into your process rather than treating it as background: a written consent script that explains what is collected, what it reveals and how long you keep it, plus a retention policy you actually follow. That satisfies §3.0 and is good practice anyway. Two communication rules matter as much as the tooling: never describe a clean result as proof of safety, and never deliver a positive result to a journalist without a plan for what happens next — device replacement, account recovery, legal and psychological support.
maintenance_evidence: GitHub API 2026-11-17: archived=false, pushed_at 2026-11-17, latest release v2026.11.2 (2026-11-02), 16,096 stars, 66 open issues. Same-day commits with date-versioned releases; institutional lineage and an active indicator-update cadence.
licence: MVT License 1.1 — NOT OSI-approved (MPL-2.0 derivative with a Consensual Use Restriction at §3.0); GitHub reports NOASSERTION
model_or_data_licence: Indicators of compromise come from Amnesty and other publishers under their own terms.
licence_restrictions: §3.0 Consensual Use Restriction (verbatim): use is permitted provided 'the Data Owner must explicitly consent to the procedure, free from any form of coercion, and must be fully informed about the nature of the procedure, its privacy implications, and any data retention and disposal policy.' Non-consensual forensic acquisition is prohibited. The restriction flows downstream on redistribution, and MPL-style file-level copyleft also applies.
costs: No fee. A forensic workstation and storage for backups (phone backups are tens of GB each). The real cost is skilled analyst time per examination plus the consent and support process around it. Estimate.
privacy: Processing is local, which is essential since a phone backup is the most intimate dataset a journalist will ever hand you. The obligations are correspondingly serious: encrypted storage, a short retention period, documented disposal, and access limited to the examining analyst. The licence makes several of these contractual rather than optional.
alternatives: androidqf for Android acquisition before MVT analysis
iLEAPP and ALEAPP for broader artefact parsing beyond spyware indicators
Referral to Amnesty Security Lab, Access Now's Digital Security Helpline or Citizen Lab where the stakes are high and in-house capacity is thin
blockers: MVT License 1.1 §3.0 consensual-use restriction — written informed consent and a disclosed retention policy are contractual requirements, and the licence is not OSI-approved
summary: Forensic toolkit that acquires and analyses iOS backups and filesystem dumps and Android device data…
oss_detail: Source published under a restricted, non-OSI licence

name: androidqf
purpose: Android Quick Forensics: a cross-platform tool that rapidly collects a standard set of forensic artefacts from an Android device over ADB — installed packages, processes, settings, logs and selected files — for later analysis.
journalism_use_case: The acquisition step for Android device checks: collect a consistent artefact set from a journalist's or source's phone in minutes, then analyse it with MVT. Android acquisition is otherwise ad hoc, and consistency is what makes results comparable across devices and over time.
pros: Standardised collection makes Android checks repeatable and comparable, which matters when you examine many devices or re-examine one over time
Fast and field-practical: a single binary over ADB, no jailbreak or root required for the standard artefact set
Same licence family and project as MVT, so acquisition and analysis are designed together
Maintained (v1.8.3, 2026-05-12; pushed 2026-11-07) with a small backlog (18 open issues)
cons: Same MVT License 1.1 consensual-use restriction as MVT, verified from the licence blob — informed consent and retention disclosure are contractual obligations, and the licence is not OSI-approved
Android's model limits what is collectable without root, so the artefact set is shallower than an iOS backup — meaning a sophisticated implant is more likely to be missed on Android than on iOS
Release cadence is slower than MVT's (v1.8.3 from May 2026 against MVT's November release), so pairing versions needs attention
Small community (387 stars); interpreting collected artefacts still requires MVT plus forensic literacy
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented: 387 stars with 18 open issues, release v1.8.3 (2026-05-12), pushed 2026-11-07, MVT License 1.1 (same licence blob text as MVT, read 2026-11-17 and recorded in leads.md L1). Session 1's ground_truth.tsv independently recorded the same licence and release.
assessment: Adopt it as the Android acquisition step whenever you run device checks — the consistency is worth it and there is no better open option. For your profile, carry the same consent process as MVT (the licence requires it identically) and be explicit with Android users that the check is shallower than an iPhone check, because that honesty matters when you report a clean result. Where the stakes are high, escalate Android cases to a specialist lab rather than relying on a quick collection.

licence_restrictions: Identical to MVT: explicit, uncoerced, fully informed consent from the Data Owner, including disclosure of privacy implications and the data retention and disposal policy. Non-consensual acquisition is prohibited.
costs: No fee. ADB-capable workstation and storage for collected artefacts. Analyst time dominates. Estimate.
privacy: Local collection and storage. The collected set is sensitive personal data about the device owner, so encrypted storage, short retention and documented disposal are required — contractually as well as ethically under this licence.
